channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: 7 simple ways to turn a new workout routine into a lasting habit
item.description: Have you started a new workout routine only to watch it fizzle out a few weeks later?

item.title: High levels of indoor radon linked to higher risk of heart failure in postmenopausal women
item.description: New findings from a study of women who have gone through menopause suggest that those living in areas with higher estimated indoor radon levels may be at higher risk of heart failure. The study, published in JAMA Network Open, was led by researchers at the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health and adds the newest evidence that radon exposure may pose a significant risk to heart health among aging women.

item.title: Hybrid light method reveals how camera signals can probe blood flow in deeper tissues
item.description: How can we efficiently collect light returning from tissues while also identifying what it tells us about blood flow in the deeper tissues? Conventional interferometric near-infrared spectroscopy (iNIRS) can distinguish signals according to the amount of time that light takes to travel through tissue, but it collects only a few photons. Camera-based systems capture many more photons, but this distinction is not realized when living tissue changes rapidly. Researchers associated with ICTER combined both approaches in a hybrid system. They showed that an appropriately analyzed camera signal can reproduce the blood-flow response observed with iNIRS for late-arriving photons, which are more sensitive to deeper tissues.

item.title: Kidney care trial challenges default dialysis planning for older adults with frailty
item.description: Dialysis should not necessarily be regarded as the default option for older people with kidney failure, the first randomized study of its kind in the world, led by the University of Bristol, has found.

item.title: Engineered protein that cuts Alzheimer's-linked brain deposits opens potential therapeutic avenue
item.description: A KAIST-led research team has found that a protein involved in gene regulation can suppress the harmful aggregation of amyloid-beta, a peptide associated with Alzheimer's disease. The approach also reduced the toxicity of protein aggregates that had already formed.

item.title: Two 'forever chemicals' associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in analysis
item.description: Women with higher blood levels of two common per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also familiarly known as PFAS, were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer, according to a new study by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in common consumer products. Often referred to as "forever chemicals," PFAS do not break down easily in the environment and can remain in the body for years.

item.title: Neural signaling protein could be therapeutic target for autism-linked gene deletion
item.description: A particular signaling protein in the brain could be a therapeutic target for neurological disorders arising from the deletion of the autism-linked gene MEF2C, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers found in a new mouse study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

item.title: Personalized vaccine targets melanoma recurrence
item.description: A personalized cancer vaccine could help prevent melanoma from returning after surgery. Sutter investigators Dr. Kevin Kim, oncologist and chief of precision medicine at Sutter Health, and Dr. Mohammed Kashani-Sabet, medical director of Sutter CPMC's Cancer Center, led Sutter's participation in the phase 2 KEYNOTE-942 study that helped make possible this advance.

item.title: AHA: Cannabis use linked to increased odds of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
item.description: Cannabis use is associated with increased odds of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in specific subgroups, including never-smokers, women and young adults without traditional risk factors, according to a study presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held from Nov. 6 to 9 in Chicago.

item.title: New study warns of dangers behind AI chatbots and 'concerning' health advice from private clinics
item.description: AI chatbots are directing users to potentially misleading health information pushed by private medical providers, according to a new Simon Fraser University study published in BMJ Connections Digital Health & AI.

item.title: COVID-19-related stress linked to faster epigenetic aging in adolescents
item.description: The COVID-19 pandemic and its associated measures caused significant stress across all levels of society, negatively impacting physical and mental health. The biological consequences of this stress have not yet been explored. Researchers found impacts at the epigenetic level, especially among adolescents. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

item.title: Child dies of measles in Wisconsin's first such death since 1990
item.description: An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state's first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.

item.title: When doctors and AI medical opinions diverge, humans must question the difference, according to experts
item.description: The human doctor and the artificial intelligence (AI) tool they are using more and more frequently are not always going to agree.

item.title: COVID-19 vaccines generated trillions in benefits, far exceeding their estimated costs
item.description: Every dollar spent on COVID-19 vaccine development and distribution generated an estimated $81 to $810 in economic value during the first year that vaccines were given, according to new research published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

item.title: Virtual reality tied to lower presurgery anxiety in kids
item.description: Children who used a virtual reality (VR) headset before surgery showed reduced self-reported distress and fear, along with lower heart rate and blood pressure, according to a new study published Nov. 5 in the journal PLOS Digital Health by Dayanjan Wijesinghe of Virginia Commonwealth University, U.S., and colleagues.

item.title: Putty-like electrode could improve vocal rehabilitation
item.description: A team of McGill University researchers has developed a putty-like electrode that molds to the skin to improve treatment and monitoring of voice disorders and upper airway diseases. In a proof-of-concept study, the sensor matched a standard clinical electrode for noise and stability while recording activity from small neck muscles.

item.title: 'Gatekeeper' cells can restrict the immune response to cancer
item.description: A new study led by King's College London has found that chemotherapy helps attract a specific population of immune cells called stem-like T cells toward tumors. The research, published in Cell Stem Cell, found that macrophages around tumor blood vessels can act as a barrier, limiting the T cells' ability to enter. By blocking an enzyme called heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) in these macrophages, the researchers were able to reduce this barrier, allowing more stem-like T cells to enter the tumor and contribute to an antitumor immune response.

item.title: Commotio cordis: How a blow to the chest can stop the heart
item.description: A recent incident during a Spanish Segunda División game between CD Tenerife and FC Andorra resulted in the tragic death of Tenerife player Jesús de Miguel. Although no official statement has confirmed the cause of his death, some reports suggest it could have been commotio cordis. This is a rare but well-known medical condition that can cause sudden cardiac arrest after a blow to the chest.

item.title: Nasal spray duo offers relief for stubborn blocked noses without rebound congestion in early clinical trial
item.description: A blocked nose can make it difficult to sleep and taste food, and it can get really annoying after a while. Nasal decongestant sprays like oxymetazoline can provide relief, but continued use can worsen nasal obstruction by causing irritation and inflammation in the nasal passages. A recent clinical trial was on a mission to find a combination of drugs that can provide lasting relief from chronic nasal blockage without triggering rebound congestion, a type of nasal obstruction that happens when you overuse nasal decongestant sprays.

item.title: Astrocytes help sustain brain activity and blood flow during prolonged sensory stimulation
item.description: What happens in the brain when sensory stimulation continues over time—for example, while jogging, reading or listening to music? Sensory input activates specific groups of neurons, increasing their demand for oxygen and nutrients. In response, nearby blood vessels dilate and increase blood flow, a process known as neurovascular coupling. Although astrocytes—star-shaped non-neuronal cells in the brain—have long been thought to participate in this process, exactly how they contribute has remained unclear.

item.title: Study links clinical characteristics to brain network connectivity in disorders of consciousness
item.description: Predicting recovery for patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC) is exceptionally difficult due to the vast differences in injury causes and demographic backgrounds. In a new study published in The Innovation Life, researchers from the Institute of Biophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Tiantan Hospital and Capital Medical University have revealed the connection between clinical characteristics (e.g., etiology, age and time since injury) and brain network connectivity. These characteristics play a crucial role in patients' functional recovery.

item.title: 'Mini lens' grown in lab could help tackle cataracts
item.description: Scientists have found a way to grow a realistic human lens, potentially providing a new path for the treatment of cataracts, one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Researchers from Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), working with colleagues at the University of Osaka in Japan and Cardiff University, have created tiny "mini lenses" in the lab using human stem cells for the very first time.

item.title: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
item.description: People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities. In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren't blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.

item.title: Slug-inspired gel seals digestive tract fistulas in animal tests
item.description: Gastrointestinal fistulas are abnormal passages between the digestive tract and another organ or tissue. They are a common complication of surgery, trauma, inflammatory diseases and malignant tumors and can be life-threatening in severe cases.

item.title: Mammograms can do more than detect breast cancer—they also offer important clues on heart health
item.description: If you're a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of routine screening for breast cancer. But there's another reason, too.

item.title: EARLY-PREG enables day-by-day tracking of thousands of proteins in the female reproductive tract
item.description: A study by MELISA Institute, published in Scientific Reports, shows how researchers can track thousands of proteins in cervicovaginal fluid over seven consecutive days. By analyzing samples collected daily from the same women, the team could compare how well two workflows detected changes in protein abundance.

item.title: New NHS-ready medication risk tool could cut falls and delirium in older people
item.description: Researchers have developed a new tool to help doctors and pharmacists identify older patients at risk of delirium and serious falls associated with taking multiple anticholinergic medications.

item.title: Lower immunity after lockdown likely impacted outbreak of deadly strep A infections
item.description: Researchers studying the winter 2022/2023 outbreak of group A streptococcus infections in Scotland have found strong evidence that the outbreak was not caused by a new virulent strain of the bacteria, but was likely the result of pandemic isolation precautions.

item.title: An ADHD diagnosis can be a map to guide a person through challenging territory—not to avoid it altogether
item.description: Picture a young person who walks out of my office with a new ADHD diagnosis and feels relief. There is finally a name for years of missed deadlines and unfinished paperwork.

item.title: Scientists use AI to develop bird flu vaccine that outperforms current stockpiled shot
item.description: A University of Cambridge team has had a third success with its AI-guided technique for designing vaccines against highly infectious viruses that threaten animal and human health. Its new broad-spectrum bird flu vaccine gave complete protection against globally circulating, diverse variants of the disease in animal trials.
